lead: Replication keeps the same data on several machines. It buys availability, low latency, read throughput and fault tolerance, and it charges one awkward question: when a client reads, which copy answers? A consistency model is the contract that settles this — it names the values a read may return, given the writes that came before. A bank balance shown in a UPI app must behave like one number; a cricket score or a social feed can lag a second and nobody minds. Choosing the model is choosing that trade.
prereq: You need: 5.6 for replicated process groups and safe message retries, and Unit 4 for happened-before and causal ordering.

sections.h3: Why replicate, and what the contract says

blocks.text: A replica is a copy of a data item kept on a second machine. It gives four gains: availability (a dead replica is covered by its peers), latency (a copy sits near the user), read throughput (reads spread over N replicas) and fault tolerance (a lost disk is not a lost record). The cost is a coordination question.

A model is defined over a history: read and write operations on data items, each issued by a process and ordered by that process's program order, plus, in real-time models, by wall-clock time. Strong models allow few answers and cost messages or waiting; weak models allow many answers and answer fast from a local copy.

items: Data-centric model: a rule for the whole store, saying in which order clients see writes.
Client-centric model: a rule for one client session, saying what that client may see.
Update protocol: the mechanism that carries a write to replicas — primary-based or quorum-based.

blocks.text: An IRCTC seat count on the payment page must be linearizable: two people must not both pay for the last seat. A live cricket score on a phone can be eventual.
Order the models by how much reordering each one permits. Every step down removes an ordering constraint, so more reads can be served from a nearby replica.

head: Model
Guarantee
rows: Read returns the latest write, even while the write is in progress.
One global order, consistent with real time.
One global order; each process's own order kept; real time ignored.
Order respects happened-before only; concurrent writes may appear in different orders.
Writes from one process stay in order; writes from different processes are unordered.
Data is consistent only after a synchronisation point.
Writes before a release are seen by any read after the matching acquire.
If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value.

blocks.text: Linearizability is what engineers mean by strong: each operation looks instantaneous at some point between its start and its end, and the order agrees with real time. Sequential consistency keeps a single global order but drops real time, so process P can read an old value after a write has finished, provided every process sees that same order. Causal consistency keeps only happened-before, so two concurrent writes may be seen in different orders at different replicas. Release consistency splits access into acquire and release phases and is what a lock-protected shared variable needs. Eventual consistency is the weakest useful promise: once writes stop, replicas agree.
A mobile client wants guarantees about itself, not about the world. Three are standard.

items: Read-your-writes: after a process writes x, its own later reads of x see that value or newer.
Monotonic reads: successive reads by one process never go back to an older version.
Writes-follow-reads: a write issued after reading x is applied to at least that version of x.

blocks.text: These are packaged as session guarantees. A load balancer that sends each request to an arbitrary replica breaks all three; pinning a session to one replica or carrying a version token keeps them.

Primary-based protocols use one replica as the primary. In remote-write the client sends every write to the primary, which forwards it to the others; reads may be local. In local-write the primary moves to the writing client, so the write costs one hop, but the system must track where the primary is.
Replicated-write has no primary. Each item carries a version number; a client writes to W replicas and reads from R replicas.

blocks.where: N is the number of replicas; W is how many replicas must acknowledge a write; R is how many a read must contact. If R + W > N, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum, so at least one reply carries the latest version.

blocks.text: The client keeps the reply with the highest version and sends it back to any replica that answered with an older one; this is read repair. Version numbers give a total order per item. Vector clocks are needed only when writes are concurrent and must be compared, not merely ordered (Unit 4).

figure.caption: The write reaches R1 and R2 only. A read of 2 replicas must overlap that write quorum (2 + 2 > 3), so it sees version 5 and returns 10, then repairs R3; a read of 1 replica can land on R3 alone and return the stale 7.

spec.aria: Three replica boxes: R1 and R2 at version 5 with x equal 10, R3 still at version 4 with x equal 7; a two-replica read returns 10 and repairs R3, a one-replica read at R3 returns 7.

examples.question: Three replicas R1, R2, R3 hold x = 7 at version 4. N = 3, W = 2. A client writes x = 10 and the write reaches only R1 and R2. (a) A read uses R = 2 and contacts R2 and R3. What is returned and what happens next? (b) A second read uses R = 1 and hits R3 only. What is returned? (c) Justify both with R + W > N.
steps: After the write, R1 holds (version 5, x = 10) and R2 holds (version 5, x = 10); R3 still holds (version 4, x = 7).
Part (a): read quorum R = 2 contacts R2, which replies (v5, 10), and R3, which replies (v4, 7).
Check the rule: R + W = 2 + 2 = 4, and N = 3, so 4 > 3 holds and the read quorum must overlap the write quorum.
The client keeps the highest version, 5, and returns x = 10.
Read repair: the client sends (v5, 10) to R3, so R3 becomes (v5, 10).
Part (b): R + W = 1 + 2 = 3, which is not greater than N = 3, so a one-replica read need not touch the write quorum.
R3 replies (v4, 7); that version is the only one seen, so the client returns x = 7, one version stale.
examples.answer: With R = 2 the client returns x = 10 and repairs R3 to version 5; with R = 1 hitting only R3 it returns the stale x = 7, because 2 + 2 = 4 > 3 holds but 1 + 2 = 3 does not.
examples.check:
n = 3
w = 2
for r in (2, 1):
    print(r + w)
print(10)
print(7)

traps: Claiming R + W = N gives strong consistency. The rule is strict: R + W > N. Equality lets a read quorum miss the write quorum, as 1 + 2 = 3 with three replicas shows.
Calling sequential consistency stronger than linearizability. Linearizability adds real-time order; sequential consistency keeps only each process's own order.
Treating eventual consistency as no consistency. It still promises per-item ordering and convergence once writes stop; what it drops is the bound on how long staleness lasts.
Mixing client-centric and data-centric guarantees. Read-your-writes is a promise to one session, not a global order for the store.
Using a single version number where vector clocks are needed. A counter orders writes but cannot tell whether two writes were concurrent.

quiz.q: Define a consistency model in one sentence.
quiz.a: A consistency model is the contract stating which values a read may return for a given history of writes and reads on replicated data.

quiz.q: In R + W > N, what do N, W and R mean?
quiz.a: N is the number of replicas, W the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write, and R the number a read must contact.

quiz.q: Give one history allowed by sequential consistency but forbidden by linearizability.
quiz.a: Process P writes x = 1 and the write completes. Later, process Q reads x and gets the old value 0, while every process still sees one single global order. Linearizability forbids this because the write already finished in real time; sequential consistency permits it because it ignores real time.

quiz.q: A store has N = 5 replicas and uses W = 3. What is the smallest R that guarantees a read quorum meets the latest write?
quiz.a: Need R + W > N, so R + 3 > 5, giving R > 2. The smallest integer is R = 3. Check: 3 + 3 = 6 > 5.

quiz.q: A client writes x = 4, then reads x from a replica still holding x = 4's previous value 2. Which client-centric guarantee is violated?
quiz.a: Read-your-writes is violated: the client's own later read of x must see its own write 4 or newer.

quiz.q: Why is eventual consistency acceptable for a cricket score but not for a bank balance?
quiz.a: A cricket score is read-only for viewers and a one-second lag changes nothing important, so cheap local reads win. A bank balance drives debits and credits; a stale read lets the same money be spent twice, so the read must see the latest write. That needs linearizability, which costs coordination and higher latency.

quiz.q: Why does remote-write make read-your-writes easy but local-write harder?
quiz.a: With remote-write the primary is fixed, so a client that reads from the primary always sees its own write. With local-write the primary moves to the writer, so a later read must be directed to the current primary; if the client reads elsewhere it can miss its own write.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems expose these knobs directly: Cassandra lets you pick R and W per query, and Dynamo-style stores tune them per table. Primary-backup replication with a log is the basis of Raft and of most managed databases. CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) get eventual consistency without read repair, and linearizability is checked by tools such as Jepsen. Search next for: quorum consistency tuning, Raft leader lease, CRDT counters, and session guarantees in mobile sync.
